section.heading: 12.3. The Dot Product
section.paragraph: So far we have seen how to add two vectors and how to multiply a vector by a scalar. The question arises: is it possible to multiply two vectors so that their product is a useful quantity? One such product is the dot product, which we now define. Another is the cross product, which is discussed in the next section.
section.heading: The Dot Product of Two Vectors
section.paragraph: To find the dot product of vectors $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ we multiply corresponding components and add.

section.paragraph: The dot product of two vectors is a real number, not a vector. For this reason, the dot product is sometimes called the scalar product (or inner product). Although Definition 1 is given for three-dimensional vectors, the dot product of two-dimensional vectors is defined in a similar fashion:
$${\langle{a_{1},a_{2}}\rangle} \cdot {\langle{b_{1},b_{2}}\rangle} = a_{1}b_{1} + a_{2}b_{2}$$
The dot product obeys many of the laws that hold for ordinary products of real numbers. These are stated in the following theorem.

section.paragraph: The dot product $$\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}$$ can be given a geometric interpretation in terms of the angle $$\theta$$ between $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ , which is defined to be the angle between the representations of $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ that start at the origin, where $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant \pi$$ . In other words, $$\theta$$ is the angle between the line segments $$\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{OA}}$$ and $$\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{OB}}$$ in Figure 1. Note that if $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ are parallel vectors, then $$\theta = 0$$ or $$\theta = \pi$$ .

section.paragraph: Two nonzero vectors $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ are called perpendicular or orthogonal if the angle between them is $$\theta = \pi \slash 2$$ . Then Theorem 3 gives
$$\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = \left| \mathbf{a} \right|\left| \mathbf{b} \right|\cos\left( {\pi \slash 2} \right) = 0$$

and conversely if $$\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = 0$$ , then $$\cos\theta = 0$$ , so $$\theta = \pi \slash 2$$ . The zero vector $$0$$ is considered to be perpendicular to all vectors. Therefore we have the following method for determining whether two vectors are orthogonal.
Two vectors $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ are orthogonal if and only if $$\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = 0$$ .

Because $$\cos\theta > 0$$ if $$0 \leqslant \theta < \pi \slash 2$$ and $$\cos\theta < 0$$ if $$\pi \slash 2 < \theta \leqslant \pi$$ , we see that $$\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}$$ is positive for $$\theta < \pi \slash 2$$ and negative for $$\theta > \pi \slash 2$$ . We can think of $$\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}$$ as measuring the extent to which $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ point in the same direction. The dot product $$\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}$$ is positive if $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ point in the same general direction, $$0$$ if they are perpendicular, and negative if they point in generally opposite directions (see Figure 2). In the extreme case where $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ point in exactly the same direction, we have $$\theta = 0$$ , so $$\cos\theta = 1$$ and
$$\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = \left| \mathbf{a} \right|\left| \mathbf{b} \right|$$

If $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ point in exactly opposite directions, then we have $$\theta = \pi$$ and so $$\cos\theta = - 1$$ and $$\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = - \left| \mathbf{a} \right|\left| \mathbf{b} \right|$$ .

section.heading: Direction Angles and Direction Cosines
section.paragraph: The direction angles of a nonzero vector $$\mathbf{a}$$ are the angles $$\alpha$$ , $$\beta$$ , and $$\gamma$$ (in the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,\pi} \right\rbrack$$ ) that $$\mathbf{a}$$ makes with the positive $$x$$ -, $$y$$ -, and $$z$$ -axes, respectively (See Figure 3).

image.alt: Details A rectangular box and a vector are graphed in the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The rectangular box has its base on the x y plane and the back left corner of the base is at the origin. The side of the base along the positive x axis is labeled a_a. A vector, labeled vector a, begins at the origin and reaches the top right corner of the front face of the box, such that the angles between the vector and the positive x, y, and z axes are alpha, beta, and gamma, respectively.

section.paragraph: The cosines of these direction angles, $$\cos\alpha$$ , $$\cos\beta$$ , and $$\cos\gamma$$ , are called the direction cosines of the vector $$\mathbf{a}$$ . Using Corollary 6 with $$\mathbf{b}$$ replaced by $$\mathbf{i}$$ , we obtain
$$\cos\alpha = \frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{i}}{\left| \mathbf{a} \right|\left| \mathbf{i} \right|} = \frac{a_{1}}{\left| \mathbf{a} \right|}$$
(This can also be seen directly from Figure 3.)
Similarly, we also have
$${\cos\beta = \frac{a_{2}}{\left| \mathbf{a} \right|}} {\cos\gamma = \frac{a_{3}}{\left| \mathbf{a} \right|}}$$
By squaring the expressions in Equations 8 and 9 and adding, we see that
$$\cos^{2}\alpha + \cos^{2}\beta + \cos^{2}\gamma = 1$$
We can also use Equations 8 and 9 to write

$$\begin{array}{l} {\mathbf{a} = {{\langle{a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}}\rangle} = {\langle{\left| \mathbf{a} \right|\cos\alpha,\left| \mathbf{a} \right|\cos\beta,\left| \mathbf{a} \right|\cos\gamma}\rangle}}} \\ {\phantom{\mathbf{a}} = {\left| \mathbf{a} \right|{\langle{\cos\alpha,\cos\beta,\cos\gamma}\rangle}}} \end{array}$$
Therefore
$$\frac{1}{\left| \mathbf{a} \right|}\mathbf{a} = {\langle{\cos\alpha,\cos\beta,\cos\gamma}\rangle}$$
which says that the direction cosines of $$\mathbf{a}$$ are the components of the unit vector in the direction of $$\mathbf{a}$$ .

section.heading: Projections
section.paragraph: Figure 4 shows representations $$\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{PQ}}$$ and $$\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{PR}}$$ of two vectors $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ with the same initial point $$P$$ . If $$S$$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $$R$$ to the line containing $$\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{PQ}}$$ , then the vector with representation $$\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{PS}}$$ is called the vector projection of $$\mathbf{b}$$ onto $$\mathbf{a}$$ and is denoted by $${proj}_{\mathbf{a}}\mathbf{b}$$ . (You can think of it as a shadow of $$\mathbf{b}$$ ).

section.paragraph: The scalar projection of $$\mathbf{b}$$ onto $$\mathbf{a}$$ (also called the component of $$\mathbf{b}$$ along $$\mathbf{a}$$ ) is defined to be the signed magnitude of the vector projection, which is the number $$\left| \mathbf{b} \right|\cos\theta$$ , where $$\theta$$ is the angle between $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ . (See Figure 5.) This is denoted by $${comp}_{\mathbf{a}}\mathbf{b}$$ . Observe that it is negative if $$\pi \slash 2 < \theta \leqslant \pi$$ . The equation
$$\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = \left| \mathbf{a} \right|\left| \mathbf{b} \right|\cos\theta = \left| \mathbf{a} \right|\left( {\left| \mathbf{b} \right|\cos\theta} \right)$$
shows that the dot product of $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ can be interpreted as the length of $$\mathbf{a}$$ times the scalar projection of $$\mathbf{b}$$ onto $$\mathbf{a}$$ . Since
$$\left| \mathbf{b} \right|\cos\theta = \frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{\left| \mathbf{a} \right|} = \frac{\mathbf{a}}{\left| \mathbf{a} \right|} \cdot \mathbf{b}$$

the component of $$\mathbf{b}$$ along $$\mathbf{a}$$ can be computed by taking the dot product of $$\mathbf{b}$$ with the unit vector in the direction of $$\mathbf{a}$$ . We summarize these ideas as follows.

section.paragraph: Scalar projection of $$\mathbf{b}$$ onto $$\mathbf{a}$$ : $${comp}_{\mathbf{a}}\mathbf{b} = \frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{\left| \mathbf{a} \right|}$$

Vector projection of $$\mathbf{b}$$ onto $$\mathbf{a}$$ : $${{proj}_{\mathbf{a}}\mathbf{b} = \left( \frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{\left| \mathbf{a} \right|} \right)\frac{\mathbf{a}}{\left| \mathbf{a} \right|} = \frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{\left| \mathbf{a} \right|^{2}}\mathbf{a}}$$
Notice that the vector projection is the scalar projection times the unit vector in the direction of $$\mathbf{a}$$ .

section.heading: Application: Work
section.paragraph: One use of projections occurs in physics in calculating work. In Section 6.4 we defined the work done by a constant force $$F$$ in moving an object through a distance $$d$$ as $$W = Fd$$ , but this applies only when the force is directed along the line of motion of the object. Suppose, however, that the constant force is a vector $$\mathbf{F} = \overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{PR}}$$ pointing in some other direction, as illustrated in Figure 6. If the force moves the object from $$P$$ to $$Q$$ , then the displacement vector is $$\mathbf{D} = \overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{PQ}}$$ . The work done by this force is defined to be the product of the component of the force along $$\mathbf{D}$$ and the distance moved:
$$W = \left( {\left| \mathbf{F} \right|\cos\theta} \right)\left| \mathbf{D} \right|$$

image.alt: Details The figure displays three vectors beginning from a common point and a line segment. The first vector begins from a point P, and runs horizontally to the right until a point Q at a distance D from P. The second vector, labeled F, begins at P, slopes upward to the right at an angle theta with the first vector, until it reaches a point R. From R, a dashed vertical line segment descends downward to meet P Q at a point S. The third vector begins at P, runs along with P Q until it reaches S.

section.paragraph: But then, from Theorem 3, we have
$$W = \left| \mathbf{F} \right|\left| \mathbf{D} \right|\cos\theta = \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{D}$$
Thus the work done by a constant force $$\mathbf{F}$$ is the dot product $$\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{D}$$ , where $$\mathbf{D}$$ is the displacement vector.
